---
title: "How Much Longer Does a Bigger Turn Take? Mental Rotation Across Eight Datasets"
description: |
  Shepard and Metzler's 1971 finding that response time grows linearly with
  rotation angle is one of the best-known results in cognitive psychology. Using
  the eight chronometric tables in the IRW's mental rotation collection, we
  estimate the slope in each and ask how much it varies across studies and
  across people.
date: today

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| echo: false

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(plotly)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 13))
irw_blue <- "#2166ac"
irw_red  <- "#d73027"
show_plot <- function(p) if (Sys.getenv("STATIC_FIGS") == "1") p else ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text")

res <- readRDS("mental_rotation_data/mental_rotation_results.rds")
date_run <- as.Date(res$computed_at)
s <- res$summary
f0 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 0)
f1 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1)
f2 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
labels <- c(
  bauer_2021_mr_pupil        = "Bauer et al. (cubes)",
  ebert_2024_animal_mr       = "Ebert et al. (animals, ages 4-6)",
  ganis_kievit_2015_mr       = "Ganis & Kievit (new 3D shapes)",
  liu_lourenco_2026_mr       = "Liu & Lourenco (3D shapes)",
  jost_2023_mr_visualization = "Jost & Siebertz (cubes)",
  jost_2022_mcmr_e1          = "Jost Exp 1 (cubes)",
  jost_2022_mcmr_e2          = "Jost Exp 2 (cubes)",
  dd_rotation                = "Borst et al. (3D shapes)")
s$label <- labels[s$table]
s$sample <- ifelse(grepl("Children", s$sample), "Children 4-6", "Adults")
m <- res$meta_rt
pooled <- as.numeric(m$b); pooled_lo <- m$ci.lb; pooled_hi <- m$ci.ub
tau <- sqrt(m$tau2)
sd_people <- res$spread$median_sd_between_people_ms_deg

# Results from data the IRW does not host (mental_rotation_external.R)
ext <- readRDS("mental_rotation_data/mental_rotation_external.rds")
es <- ext$summary
ma <- ext$meta_all
pooled_all <- as.numeric(ma$b); pooled_all_lo <- ma$ci.lb; pooled_all_hi <- ma$ci.ub
ES <- function(t, col) es[[col]][es$table == t]
```

In 1971, Shepard and Metzler showed people pairs of drawings of 3D block figures and asked whether the two were the same object or mirror images [@shepard1971]. The time it took to answer "same" grew in a straight line with the angle between the two figures, at roughly one second for every 60 degrees, or about 17 ms per degree. It looked as though people were turning a mental image at a steady speed. The result became a textbook staple, and the task has since been run in hundreds of studies.

The IRW's `mental_rotation` collection now holds eight tables where each trial records both the response time and the rotation angle. They differ in almost every way a study can differ: 3D cube figures, new 3D shapes and animal pictures; preschoolers and adults; same/mirror judgements and "which of these two matches?" choices; ordinary lab sessions and sessions with eye tracking. That makes them a natural test of how general the linear angle effect is and how big it is.

## The data

```{r}
#| label: tbl-data
#| tbl-cap: "The eight chronometric mental rotation tables. Slope and intercept come from the mixed model described below; accuracy is over all answered trials."

s |>
  transmute(Table = paste0("`", table, "`"), Study = label, Stimuli = stimuli,
            Sample = sample, Task = format, People = n_people, Angles = angles,
            Accuracy = scales::percent(accuracy, 1)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

We also fit the same model to `r nrow(es)` chronometric datasets that the IRW does not host (@tbl-external), to see whether they tell the same story: the cross-cultural MRTX study [@ruginski2019], a small study of athletes and non-athletes, and the LEVANTE mental rotation task for children aged 5 to 12 [@levante2026], in its 2D (animal) and 3D (shape) forms. Their results are kept apart from the IRW tables in every figure below.

Sources: @bauer2021, @ebert2024, @ganis2015, @liu2026, @jost2023, @jost2022 (two experiments), and @borst2011 as distributed with @vandermaas2011. Angles are angular disparity, folded to 0–180 degrees, so a 270° turn counts as 90°.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-external
#| tbl-cap: "Datasets the IRW does not host. A separate script (`mental_rotation_external.R`) downloads each file from the depositor's repository when it runs, fits the same model, and keeps only summary results."

es |>
  transmute(Study = label, Source = source_url, `Why not in the IRW` = why_not_hosted,
            Stimuli = stimuli, Sample = sample, People = n_people, Angles = angles,
            Accuracy = scales::percent(accuracy, 1)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

## Response time rises with angle in every dataset

```{r}
#| label: fig-curves
#| fig-cap: "Median response time on correct trials at each rotation angle. Each line is one table."

ba <- bind_rows(
  res$by_angle |> left_join(s |> select(table, label), by = "table") |> mutate(hosted = "IRW table"),
  ext$by_angle |> left_join(es |> select(table, label), by = "table") |> mutate(hosted = "Not hosted by the IRW"))
p <- ggplot(ba, aes(angle, median_rt, colour = label, group = label, linetype = hosted,
                    text = paste0(label, "<br>", angle, "°: ", f2(median_rt), " s (", n, " trials)"))) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Rotation angle (degrees)", y = "Median correct RT (s)", colour = NULL, linetype = NULL)
show_plot(p)
```

The lines sit at different heights; the two Jost multiple-choice experiments in particular are slower overall (about 5 s at their easiest angle), since each screen is part of a longer test with a time limit per block. What matters for the classic finding is the shape, and every line rises. Most rise roughly steadily; the Borst et al. data flatten between 100° and 150°, and the two Jost multiple-choice experiments between 135° and 180°.

To put a number on the rise, we fit the same model to every table: response time on correct trials (between 0.2 and 15 s) regressed on angle, with a random intercept and a random angle slope for each person and a random intercept for each item:

$$\text{RT}_{pi} = (\beta_0 + u_{0p} + v_i) + (\beta_1 + u_{1p})\,\text{angle}_i + \varepsilon_{pi}$$

$\beta_1$ is the typical slope in the study, and the spread of $u_{1p}$ says how much people within the study differ from it.

```{r}
#| label: fig-forest
#| fig-cap: "Slope of response time on rotation angle (ms per degree) in each dataset, with 95% intervals, and random-effects pooled estimates with and without the datasets the IRW does not host (grey). The dashed line marks Shepard and Metzler's roughly 17 ms per degree."

fd <- bind_rows(s |> mutate(kind = "IRW table"), es |> mutate(kind = "Not hosted by the IRW")) |>
  mutate(lo = slope_ms_deg - 1.96 * slope_se, hi = slope_ms_deg + 1.96 * slope_se) |>
  arrange(kind == "IRW table", slope_ms_deg)
fd <- bind_rows(fd,
  tibble(label = "Pooled, IRW tables", slope_ms_deg = pooled, lo = pooled_lo, hi = pooled_hi, kind = "Pooled"),
  tibble(label = paste0("Pooled, all ", nrow(s) + nrow(es), " datasets"), slope_ms_deg = pooled_all, lo = pooled_all_lo, hi = pooled_all_hi, kind = "Pooled"))
fd$label <- factor(fd$label, levels = fd$label)
p <- ggplot(fd, aes(slope_ms_deg, label, xmin = lo, xmax = hi,
                    text = paste0(label, ": ", f1(slope_ms_deg), " ms/°  [", f1(lo), ", ", f1(hi), "]"))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1000 / 60, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_errorbarh(height = 0.2, colour = irw_blue) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = kind), size = 2.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`IRW table` = irw_blue, `Not hosted by the IRW` = "grey55", Pooled = irw_red), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Slope (ms per degree)", y = NULL)
show_plot(p)
```

Every slope is clearly positive. Pooled across the eight tables, response time rises by **`r f1(pooled)` ms per degree** (95% CI `r f1(pooled_lo)` to `r f1(pooled_hi)`), about half of Shepard and Metzler's figure. Adding the `r nrow(es)` datasets the IRW does not host gives `r f1(pooled_all)` ms per degree (`r f1(pooled_all_lo)` to `r f1(pooled_all_hi)`). The large cross-cultural MRTX study, with `r f0(ES("external_mrtx", "n_people"))` people aged 5 to 84 at six field sites, comes in at `r f1(ES("external_mrtx", "slope_ms_deg"))` ms per degree. The one dataset near Shepard and Metzler's value is LEVANTE's 3D task: `r f0(ES("external_levante_3d", "n_people"))` children rotating 3D shapes slow down by `r f1(ES("external_levante_3d", "slope_ms_deg"))` ms per degree, about twice as steeply as the same children rotating 2D animal silhouettes (`r f1(ES("external_levante_2d", "slope_ms_deg"))` ms per degree). Stimulus complexity seems to matter more for the slope than age does: the preschoolers judging animal pictures in the IRW's Ebert et al. table have one of the shallowest slopes. A turn of 90° adds a bit under a second, not a second and a half. The slowest rotators are the preschoolers in @ebert2024 at `r f1(s$slope_ms_deg[s$table == "ebert_2024_animal_mr"])` ms per degree; the steepest slopes, around 11 ms per degree, come from adults rotating cube figures.

Several things could pull the slope below the classic value. Shepard and Metzler's eight participants each did 1,600 trials, many more than in any of these studies. Several of these studies use simpler shapes or picture stimuli. And our model averages same and mirror trials, where the original slope was for "same" pairs only. Whatever the reason, a figure near 8–9 ms per degree looks like a better default expectation for a modern study than 17.

## People differ more than studies do

The studies do differ in their slopes: the random-effects model puts the standard deviation of true study slopes at **`r f1(tau)` ms per degree**, far more than sampling error would produce. But within a typical study, people's own slopes vary with a standard deviation of about **`r f1(sd_people)` ms per degree**. The difference between two people in the same study is usually larger than the difference between two studies.

```{r}
#| label: fig-people
#| fig-cap: "Each person's estimated slope (fixed slope plus their random effect), by table. Points are people; the black bar is the table's fixed slope."

pp <- res$person |> left_join(s |> select(table, label, slope_ms_deg), by = "table")
pp$label <- factor(pp$label, levels = s$label[order(s$slope_ms_deg)])
p <- ggplot(pp, aes(slope_ms_deg.x, label, text = paste0(label, "<br>person slope ", f1(slope_ms_deg.x), " ms/°"))) +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.2, alpha = 0.25, size = 0.8, colour = irw_blue) +
  geom_point(aes(slope_ms_deg.y, label), shape = 124, size = 6, colour = "black") +
  labs(x = "Person slope (ms per degree)", y = NULL)
show_plot(p)
```

These person slopes are shrunken estimates, so the true spread is, if anything, larger than the picture shows. The Borst et al. table is the exception: with only three angles, ten items and a flat stretch between 100° and 150°, the model cannot separate people's slopes at all (the person-slope variance is estimated at essentially zero), and its own slope comes with a wide interval.

In every table, people who are slower overall also tend to have steeper slopes: the correlation between person intercepts and person slopes is positive throughout, from `r f2(min(s$r_intercept_slope[s$table != "dd_rotation"]))` to `r f2(max(s$r_intercept_slope[s$table != "dd_rotation"]))` (leaving out the Borst et al. table, where the slope variance collapses). Being slow at mental rotation is partly being slow at the rotation itself, not only at encoding the figures or pressing the key.

## Does age matter?

Some of the spread in @fig-forest could be age: the IRW's shallowest slope comes from preschoolers [@ebert2024], and the external datasets range from 4-year-olds to people in their 80s. Comparing studies cannot separate age from everything else that differs between them, so we look instead inside the two studies that span a wide range of ages, fitting the same model separately within each age band.

```{r}
#| label: fig-age
#| fig-cap: "Slope of response time on rotation angle by age band, within the MRTX study (ages 5-84) and the LEVANTE mental rotation task (ages 4-13, 2D and 3D items), with 95% intervals. Each point is a separate model fit to the people in that band. Neither dataset is hosted by the IRW."

ab <- ext$age_bands |>
  mutate(hi = as.numeric(sub(".*,([0-9.]+)\\)$", "\\1", band)),
         mid = (lo + pmin(hi, 70)) / 2,
         l95 = slope_ms_deg - 1.96 * slope_se, u95 = slope_ms_deg + 1.96 * slope_se)
p <- ggplot(ab, aes(mid, slope_ms_deg, colour = study, group = study,
                    text = paste0(study, ", ages ", band, ": ", f1(slope_ms_deg), " ms/° (", n_people, " people)"))) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1000 / 60, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = l95, ymax = u95), position = position_dodge(width = 1)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(5, 10, 15, 25, 40, 60)) +
  labs(x = "Age (years; band midpoint)", y = "Slope (ms per degree)", colour = NULL)
show_plot(p)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
AB <- function(st, b, col = "slope_ms_deg") ab[[col]][startsWith(ab$study, st) & ab$band == b]
```

Within studies, the youngest children have the shallowest slopes. In LEVANTE's 2D task, the slope rises from `r f1(AB("LEVANTE 2D", "[4,7)"))` ms per degree in 4- to 6-year-olds to `r f1(AB("LEVANTE 2D", "[11,14)"))` in 11- to 13-year-olds, and the 3D task shows the same rise from a higher starting point. MRTX shows an inverted U: slopes climb from childhood to a peak in the teens (`r f1(AB("MRTX", "[13,18)"))` ms per degree) and fall again across adulthood, to `r f1(AB("MRTX", "[50,90)"))` among people over 50. So age does account for some of the spread in @fig-forest. The preschool table sits low, and MRTX, with the oldest participants of any study here, comes in below the pooled value.

Stimuli matter more, though. At every age, LEVANTE's children are roughly twice as steep on 3D shapes as on 2D animal silhouettes, a bigger gap than separates any two age bands within one task.

A shallow slope in young children should not be read as faster rotation. Young children (and, in MRTX, older adults) are also less accurate, and the model uses correct trials only. When accuracy is low, some correct answers at large angles are quick guesses, which pulls the slope down. A model that handles speed and accuracy together, such as a diffusion model, would be needed to separate how fast people rotate from how carefully they respond.

## Accuracy falls too

```{r}
#| label: fig-accuracy
#| fig-cap: "Proportion correct at each rotation angle, by table."

p <- ggplot(ba, aes(angle, accuracy, colour = label, group = label,
                    text = paste0(label, "<br>", angle, "°: ", scales::percent(accuracy, 1)))) +
  geom_line() + geom_point() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Rotation angle (degrees)", y = "Proportion correct", colour = NULL)
show_plot(p)
```

Larger rotations are not just slower; they are also more often answered wrongly. A logistic mixed model of accuracy on angle (random intercepts for people and items) gives a negative angle effect in every table (the curves are not all monotone; the Jost multiple-choice experiments wobble at 180°), pooling to `r f2(as.numeric(res$meta_acc$b))` on the logit scale per 100 degrees. So the time cost of rotation does not buy back full accuracy: people do not simply rotate until they are sure.

## Caveats

**One trimming rule and one model for all tables.** We keep correct trials between 0.2 and 15 s and fit RT in seconds on a linear scale. The depositors used their own outlier rules, and some analyses use log RT. These choices change individual slopes somewhat but not the picture that every slope is positive and the pooled value is near 8–9 ms per degree.

**Same and mirror trials are pooled**, and so are tasks with different response formats (same/mirror judgements versus choosing which of two figures matches). The "pick the match" tasks in the Jost tables involve comparing two candidates, which may add a constant rather than change the slope, but we have not separated these.

**The tables are not a random sample of studies.** They are the chronometric mental rotation datasets we could find with an open licence and trial-level data, and five of the eight come from one research group (Petra Jansen's and Leonardo Jost's). More tables would sharpen the between-study estimate in particular.

**Data the IRW does not host.** `mental_rotation_external.R` downloads the MRTX and athletes/non-athletes files from OSF each time it runs and deletes them afterwards, and reads the LEVANTE trials from Redivis; only the estimates shown here are stored with the page, and for LEVANTE not even person-level slopes are kept. The MRTX file is openly licensed but identifies participants by name, the athletes study sets no licence, and LEVANTE's Data Use Agreement forbids redistribution, so none of them can be added to the IRW. Their results are shown for comparison and are not part of the IRW pooled estimate.

**LEVANTE.** Results use the LEVANTE Data Repository release levante-data-pilots v4.0 (doi:10.57761/fwqx-vx48), accessed under its Data Use Agreement; rerunning that part needs a Redivis account approved under the agreement. The task was given in fixed and adaptive forms across several task versions, so in the adaptive runs the angles a child saw depended on how they were doing. The LEVANTE sites differ in sampling and administration, and as the agreement notes, differences between sites are not estimates of differences between countries; we do not compare sites here.

**The Borst et al. angles come from documentation.** The `dd_rotation` table now carries an `itemcov_angle` column, taken from the diffIRT package documentation that accompanies the data.

Results computed `r format(date_run, "%B %d, %Y")`. All eight IRW tables are fetched with `irw::irw_fetch()`. The two external datasets are downloaded from OSF by a separate script and are not stored here. To regenerate (a few minutes):

```r
Rscript vignettes/mental_rotation_compute.R    # IRW tables
Rscript vignettes/mental_rotation_external.R   # data the IRW does not host
quarto::quarto_render("vignettes/mental_rotation.qmd")
```
